title: About text8-word2vec
tagline: Three embeddings trained on the same 17M words of Wikipedia (CBOW, skip-gram, fastText) next to GloVe's 6 billion: neighbours, analogies, similarity and a map.

sections.title: The Problem
body: Count-based vectors (the previous demo, 3b) treat every word as its own column. "great" and "excellent" are as unrelated as "great" and "boring", and the vectors grow with the vocabulary.

Word embeddings give every word a short, dense vector (here 100 numbers) learned from the words around it, so words used in similar contexts end up close together. This demo trains three kinds of embedding on the same Wikipedia text and puts them next to a much larger pretrained model, so you can probe what each one learned.

sections.title: Approach — Why Compare CBOW, Skip-gram and fastText?
body: Lecture 5 of the End-to-End NLP course introduces Word2Vec and its two training methods. CBOW and skip-gram are not two different models: they are two ways of training the **same** Word2Vec network. fastText adds one idea on top of skip-gram. All three here are trained on the same {{split.corpus_tokens}} words of text8 with the same settings, so any difference comes from the method.
GloVe 6B is included as a fixed reference. It was trained by Stanford on 6 billion words (about 350 times more), so it shows what scale buys.

bullets.label: Why 100 dimensions, window 5
bullets.text: The common defaults. Every model, including GloVe, uses 100-d vectors so they are compared like for like.

bullets.label: Why min_count 5
bullets.text: Words seen fewer than five times are dropped: there is too little context to learn a useful vector.

bullets.label: Why trained offline
bullets.text: Training all three takes about 35 minutes on the NAS CPU, too long to repeat on every container restart. A script trains them once, logs the run to MLflow and saves the vectors; the service loads them in seconds.

bullets.label: Why a smaller fastText
bullets.text: fastText hashes character pieces into a table. gensim's default table made an 830 MB model; 200,000 rows keeps it near 110 MB.

sections.title: From Raw Text to Numbers
body: text8 comes pre-cleaned: Matt Mahoney reduced the first 100 MB of an English Wikipedia dump to lowercase letters a–z and single spaces, with numbers spelled out. So the only step here is splitting on spaces.

Then comes the part that differs from 3b: instead of counting words, each model **learns** a vector per word by trying to predict words from their neighbours. The vector is a by-product of that prediction task.

sections.title: How Word2Vec Learns
body: Slide a window over the text. In "the **king** wore a crown", the centre word is *king* and the context is *the, wore, a, crown*. A tiny network with one hidden layer of 100 units is trained on millions of these windows. The hidden-layer weights for each word become its vector.

Training compares the true word with a handful of random "negative" words and nudges vectors so the true pair scores higher (negative sampling, 5 negatives here). That is what makes training on millions of windows affordable.

bullets.label: CBOW
bullets.text: Averages the context words and predicts the centre word. Fast, because each window is one prediction. Tends to smooth over rare words. Trained in {{comparison.cbow.train_time}}.

bullets.label: Skip-gram
bullets.text: Uses the centre word to predict each context word separately. Each window becomes several predictions, so it is slower ({{comparison.skipgram.train_time}}), but rare words get more updates. Usually better on analogies and similarity.

bullets.label: fastText
bullets.text: Skip-gram where each word is also the sum of its character pieces (3 to 6 letters: "<ki", "kin", "ing>"…). Words sharing pieces share information, and a word never seen in training still gets a vector from its pieces. Trained in {{comparison.fasttext.train_time}}.

bullets.label: GloVe (reference)
bullets.text: A different recipe: it factorises a table of how often words appear together across the whole corpus, instead of sliding a window. Pretrained on 6 billion words; trimmed here to the 50,000 most frequent.

sections.title: Reading the Embedding Space
body: Closeness is measured with **cosine similarity**: 1 means the vectors point the same way, 0 means unrelated. Nearest neighbours are the words with the highest cosine similarity.

**Analogies** use vector arithmetic: king − man + woman lands near queen because the direction from *man* to *woman* is roughly the same as from *king* to *queen*. The Google analogy set splits these into meaning (capitals, currencies, family) and grammar (plurals, tenses, comparatives).

The **2-D map** squeezes 100 dimensions into 2 with PCA, fitted separately for each model and each word list. It keeps the biggest differences and loses the rest, so read clusters, not exact distances.

sections.title: Model Architecture
body: Each trained model is a 100-d vector per word for the {{comparison.cbow.vocabulary_size}} words seen at least five times in text8. fastText also keeps 200,000 × 100 vectors for hashed character pieces. GloVe keeps its 50,000 most frequent words. The service memory-maps the saved vectors, so only the pages a query touches are read into RAM.

sections.title: Service Architecture
body: Same per-project 4-layer pattern (ADR-013) used by every project on pandyaHomeLab. The browser sends a word, an analogy, a word pair or a word list; the server answers from all four models at once. Training is not part of the running service: it happens offline and only its saved vectors are mounted in.

sections.title: Network & Deployment
body: The NLP domain has its own bridge network (ADR-016). Only nlp-mlflow runs alongside the demos: postgres, MinIO and Redis have reserved addresses but are not deployed until a demo needs one (Phase 3 gate G1). The tracker is public, read-only, at `mlflow-nlp.pandyahomelab.com`.
No cross-network reach-back into ml-network or dl-network — each domain's tracking and demos are independent.

sections.title: Dataset
body: **text8**: the first 10^8 bytes of an English Wikipedia dump from 2006, cleaned by Matt Mahoney to lowercase letters and spaces. It is the corpus the original Word2Vec tools use for their demos: small enough to train on a CPU, big enough for analogies to start working. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA.

The reference is **GloVe 6B 100d** (Pennington, Socher and Manning, 2014), trained on Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5, released under the Public Domain Dedication (PDDL). Both are downloaded at pinned versions and checked against SHA-256 checksums.
Evaluation uses the **Google analogy set** (Mikolov et al., 2013; 19,544 questions) and **WordSim-353** (353 word pairs scored by people), both shipped with gensim.

sections.title: What These Models Can't Do
body: An embedding is a summary of which words appear near which. It is not a dictionary, and the summary has blind spots.

bullets.label: One vector per word
bullets.text: "bank" (river) and "bank" (money) share one vector, blended by how often each sense appears. Contextual models (transformers) fix this; they are planned for a later v2 demo.

bullets.label: Opposites look similar
bullets.text: "hot" and "cold" appear in the same kinds of sentences, so they end up close together. Similarity here means "used alike", not "means the same".

bullets.label: Small corpus
bullets.text: 17 million words is tiny next to GloVe's 6 billion. Rare words get noisy vectors, and many analogies fail. Compare the trained columns with the GloVe column.

bullets.label: Unseen words
bullets.text: CBOW and skip-gram have no vector for a word they never saw (try "moviee"). fastText makes one from spelling, which works for typos and word forms but can produce confident nonsense for unrelated words that merely look alike.

bullets.label: Bias
bullets.text: The vectors absorb the associations in their text, including social stereotypes present in 2006 Wikipedia and in news text.

bullets.label: Old text
bullets.text: text8 is a 2006 snapshot. Anything newer is missing.

sections.title: Performance
sections.problem_type: Unsupervised representation learning · intrinsic evaluation (analogies + similarity)
body: Embeddings have no labels to score against, so they are judged on two standard tests. Every model is asked the same questions over its {{metrics_display.analogy_vocab}} most frequent words; a question with a word outside that vocabulary counts as not attempted.

metrics_detail.name: Analogy accuracy · meaning
metrics_detail.what: Share of meaning analogies answered exactly: capitals (athens : greece :: paris : ?), currencies, US states, family (king : queen :: man : ?).
metrics_detail.formula: top-1 of most_similar(b + c − a) == d
metrics_detail.why_chosen: The test Mikolov et al. introduced with Word2Vec; it checks that relations became consistent directions.
metrics_detail.watch_out: All-or-nothing: the right answer at rank 2 scores zero.

metrics_detail.name: Analogy accuracy · grammar
metrics_detail.what: Share of grammar analogies answered exactly: plurals, verb tenses, comparatives, adverbs (quick : quickly :: slow : ?).
metrics_detail.formula: top-1 of most_similar(b + c − a) == d
metrics_detail.why_chosen: Split out because fastText's spelling pieces make grammar easy for it; the combined score would hide that.
metrics_detail.watch_out: High grammar scores can come from spelling alone, without learning meaning.

metrics_detail.name: WordSim-353
metrics_detail.what: Rank correlation between the model's cosine similarity and people's 0–10 similarity ratings for 353 word pairs.
metrics_detail.why_chosen: Checks graded similarity, not just exact answers.
metrics_detail.watch_out: The ratings mix "similar" with "related" (cup–coffee), and 353 pairs is a small sample.
